The most unfortunate thing about most Indians is that they have little faith in scientific study and more faith in the words of their leaders (religious and political) and the ancient scriptures. There are millions of such myths, which are totally false and unscientific, and still, hundreds of millions Indians believe in such lies. Unless Indians learn to think rationally, develop a scientific temper, and stop believing in mythologies, India can never become a happy, developed and prosperous nation.

Question: What are the reasons for the existence of corruption in some countries like India and Pakistan, while countries like Singapore and Japan have lower levels of corruption? Is it accurate to say that there is no corruption at all in Singapore and Japan?
Answer: Corruption has a negative correlation with development and economic prosperity. According to Transparency International, the list of the least and most corrupt countries in the world as of 2023 is as follows, [1] The least corrupt countries in the world The most corrupt countries in the world You can easily see that without an exception, all the least corrupt countries are the developed countries with a per capita income of $20,000 or more. Similarly, the most corrupt countries of the world are also the least developed countries whose per capita income is hardly $2000. The position of India was 93 with a CPI score of 39/100 in 2023, while that of Pakistan is 133 with a CPI Score of 29/100 in 2023. Thus, India and Pakistan are in the middle of the list of corrupt countries. Hence, it is evident that corruption can’t be removed unless the country achieves economic prosperity and becomes a developed country. Singapore and Japan are the most honest countries in Asia because they are also the most developed countries in Asia. None of the countries in the world is free from corruption, as no country has a CPI score of 10/10. The CPI scores of Singapore and Japan are 83/100 and 73/100, respectively, which means that corruption is less in these countries than in India (39/100), but these countries are still not free from corruption. Corruption and poverty are thus positively correlated Hence, it is unrealistic to assume that a country can become honest without achieving development. Since economic development is a slow process, the reduction of corruption is also a slow process. However, corruption must naturally reduce as the national economy improves and the country's per capita income rises. Unfortunately, that is not happening in India, at least after 2016. The ranking of India in 2023 was 93 (CPI 39/100), while it was 80 in 2016 (CPI 40/100), while in the same period, the per capita income of India increased from $1714 (2016) to $2411 (2022)[2]. Thus, corruption in India is increasing despite economic development due to the patronising of corruption by the elected governments in India, who have politicised and reduced the power of the anti-corruption agencies. The following data show that India's CPI score was constantly improving prior to 2016, and there was a significant improvement in the period 2012–2014[3] because, in those days, the anti-corruption agencies had more freedom to do their jobs and could arrest even the ruling party politicians and central ministers without seeking approval from the government. Since more corruption cases were booked and freely reported earlier, the popular perception then was that corruption was increasing 2012-2015. However, after 2018, when corruption actually started increasing due to amendment of Prevention of Corruption Act curbing the powers of anti-corruption agencies, the Indian public is under the impression that it is going down because corruption cases against the ruling parties are not started and not reported.

Question: Is India ready for a uniform civil code? What would be the benefits in eliminating religious personal laws? Are the concerns against it justified?
Answer: The recent statement of Indian Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi that India needed a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) as the country could not run with the dual system of “separate laws for separate communities”, has fuelled speculation for the implementation of Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in India soon. UCC has been in the manifesto of the BJP for a long time and with Modi Government commanding a majority in Parliament, there is a high possibility of UCC law being passed soon. The Uniform Civil Code means that the same law shall be applicable to all uniformly in matters of - Marriage, divorce, maintenance, inheritance, adoption and succession of property, irrespective of religion. The term, ‘Uniform Civil Code’ is explicitly mentioned in Article 44 of the Indian Constitution, which says “The State shall endeavor to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” In my opinion, UCC is good for the country as it will be in the spirit of secular India where people shall be given equal status irrespective of their religion. Objections against UCC Since UCC shall be dealing with issues like marriage, divorce, maintenance etc, which have been traditionally decided on the basis of religion, the detractors would contend that it will rob the nation of its religious diversity and violate the fundamental right to practise religion enshrined in Article 25 and Article 29 of the Constitution. They argue that UCC is a directive principle which can’t override the fundamental rights enshrined in the Constitution. Article 25 provides the freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion, while Article 29 provides that all sections of the citizens having a distinct language, script or culture of their own shall have the right to conserve the same. However, I believe that many cultures and traditions have outdated and must be discarded as soon as possible to create a modern society. For example, there is no provision for divorce and property inheritance by daughters in the Hindu religion. However, Indian laws have been implemented to provide these rights to Hindu women. In Islam, there is a provision that men can marry up to four women. Similarly, divorce provisions are much easier in Islam, and even triple talaq is permitted. Further, under Muslim personal law, maintenance was to be paid only till the period of iddat. (three lunar months-roughly 90 days ).[1] Way Ahead I don’t think that any right-minded person would support the right of a man to have four wives. The very concept appears repugnant to me, which denies dignity to women in the modern world. I also believe that women of all religions must be equally protected from arbitrary divorce and given the same compensation which can ensure them a dignified life. Surely, there will be opposition to the UCC by some people and political parties to influence their vote bank. Yet, the opponents of UCC would be in small numbers in India and those who oppose UCC may pay a heavy price for opposing this progressive move by Government. However, the drafting of UCC must be done very carefully incorporating the best practices of all religions so that no religion feels discriminated against or privileged.

Question: Is it possible for a person to completely change their habits in an instant?
Answer: I was a good student in my school days. I was not the best, as used to stand second or third in the class, but I was very righteous as I neither copied, nor liked anyone else to copy in the examination. I hated the very idea of copying and cheating in the examination because that was against the sincere student who may end up scoring lesser marks despite their hard work and superior knowledge while the cheaters can get better marks by copying. Hence, when I found someone cheating in the examination hall, I would often complain against the person to the examiner, though it angered the cheaters. When I joined my B Tech (Mechanical Engineering), in IIT-BHU (Then known as IT-BHU) Varanasi, during the internal tests, most professors allowed us the freedom to choose our seats, while in the end-semester examination, everyone was required to sit on the seats according to their roll numbers. It was fashionable for the students to occupy the seats from the last rows, where the examiner couldn’t see the students clearly, and hence one could copy the answers from the neighbour answer sheet. Since I had no intention to cheat, I used to occupy the first-row seat in the class, while my friends preferred the last seats. Some of these students scored better grades than me despite studying much lesser, and they used to laugh at me for being honest. Since these people were in large numbers and I had to live with them in the same hostel, I did not wish to antagonise them by complaining against them. So, what did I do? I followed the dictum, “If you can't beat them, join them.” One of my friends convinced me of the benefit of cheating in the examination, “Awdhesh! Copying does not mean that you stop studying. I study hard, plus I also copy from my neighbour. As a result, my score is better than yours despite having the same knowledge since what I copy from my neighbour is an extra.” I got convinced and he helped me learn the art of copying. Copying was difficult for me, but then I really discovered that I could score better marks with copying if I sat behind a smart student. So, I developed a friendship with the toppers of my class and I will ensure that I sat at the best location to copy their answers. Gradually, I developed the habit of copying in the examination. As a result, my focus on studies declined gradually, and my focus would rather be to get a seat near the best student. I also paid little attention in class. Why work hard when you can score well easily by copying? Unfortunately, my grades started declining slowly since I wasn’t lucky enough to get the right seat every time. In B Tech's 3rd year, we had a paper on ‘Automotive Control’. The professor was good but very strict. Moreover, the subject was concept-based and the lectures started going over my head very soon since I did not grasp the earlier topics. Then came the first test, or mid term. I thought I would get the right seat and score well, but unfortunately, other students already occupied the best seats near the toppers and I had to sit in the front seats. The result? I got 2/15 marks on the test. I was very disappointed but took the solace that many of my friends performed even worse. Yet everything was not lost, since we still had two more tests to go and the best two out of three was to be considered for the award of grade. I still had hopes to score well in the next two tests and make up. However, the professor was too smart. Next time, instead of taking tests in the classroom, he asked us to take the test in the drawing hall, which was very huge and we already had allotted seats, far away from each other. He also brought some of his PhD students to invigilate, which made it impossible to cheat. When I saw the paper, I was totally stunned as I did not know the answer to even one question. I was sitting there in the examination hall hoping to copy from someone, but gradually I realised that it was impossible to cheat that day. I started thinking about my younger days when I was so much against copying. I also remembered that in those days, I used to have so much command over the subject that I could solve all problems, and lost marks usually because of some silly mistakes. I felt ashamed of myself for falling so low and felt disgusted. I rose from my chair and submitted the copy, totally blank, and came out of the examination hall with the resolve that I would never cheat again in my life. And I never cheated again in any examination in my life. After the incident, I worked hard and got 11/15 on the final test and 8/10 on my assignment. However, in the end-semester examination, I got 42/60, the second highest in the class. Though my final grade in automotive control was only C as I missed a B grade marginally with a score of 63/100, I was lucky to pass the semester without any back paper, while more than half the students got back in that paper. The shame I felt about myself in the examination hall changed my life forever in an instant to get rid of my habit of copying in an instant. It takes only an instant to change your habits provided you realise your mistake. It is wisely said ,”If an egg is broken by outside force, life ends. If broken by inside force, life begins. Great things always begin from inside” Source of pictures: Google Images

Question: Richard Feynman said, “Never confuse education with intelligence, you can have a PhD and still be an idiot.” What are some real life examples of this?
Answer: Intelligence is generally defined as the ability to gather knowledge and skills and apply them to your life to solve life's complex problems. On the other hand, education requires you to get into a college and pass the examination prescribed by law to get the required degree. If you have a good memory and follow rote learning, you can easily get even the highest degree in the world with top marks. Getting a degree has become so easy in modern times that anyone with average intelligence can acquire any degree, including a PhD, provided he or she is willing to spend the desired time pursuing the degree. Most PhD holders work in universities, where a PhD is the minimum requirement to become a faculty member. However, many professors are people of average intelligence who often choose the teaching profession not as a matter of choice but because they did not get into the best jobs at their lower qualifications. Smarter people often get jobs after their BE/B Tech, MBA, LLB/LLM, MBBS/MS, etc., and have better career prospects. The smartest people don’t waste their time doing graduation but drop out of school and college and set up companies like Microsoft, Apple or Google. The wisest people in the world, like Buddha, Kabir, or Socrates did not have a college degree, but they learned their lessons from life itself using their analytical skills and keen observation. While education is helpful in acquiring knowledge, it does not make you more intelligent. Knowledge acquired from textbooks can make an intelligent person wiser and more creative, but it can also make a stupid person even more stupid. The story of ‘Four Learned Fools’ from Panchtantra illustrates how education can’t make a stupid person intelligent. In a town, there lived four friends who were quite learned. One day, they decided to leave their native place and seek their fortune in the city, which offered so many more opportunities to earn money. Packing in all their holy books, they were on their way.[1] Soon, they came to an intersection of the road and did not know which path to follow. Now, the son of a merchant had died in the town, and at that very moment, a huge funeral procession that included several prominent citizens of the town passed by. One of the friends consulted his holy scriptures and read aloud: ‘Whichever road is followed by great men is the right one to follow’. So they said, ‘Let us go the same way as these people.’ Following the road taken by the prominent citizens, the group reached the cremation ground, and saw a donkey standing there. The second friend opened his holy scriptures and read: ‘Whosoever stands by you on all occasions, whether joyous or sad, is your true friend’. So, the four friends concluded that the donkey was their true friend. Accordingly, one of the friends put his arms around the donkey’s neck; the second friend kissed him, whilst the third began to wash his hoofs. They kept chanting, ‘He is our true friend’. Just then, they saw a camel advance quickly towards them. The third friend consulted his religious book and read: ‘Righteousness marches rapidly.’ So they all agreed that the advancing camel must be nothing but righteousness incarnate. Right then, the fourth friend opened his holy scriptures and read: ‘A wise man should lead his friend to righteousness’. So they decided to introduce the donkey to the camel, and when the camel approached, they tied the two animals together. When the donkey’s master, a washerman, heard the news that his donkey was being dragged along by a camel, he picked up a stick to beat the four learned fools, who then had to run for their lives. When they had gone a little way, the foursome came upon a river. The leaf of a holy tree was floating by. One of them cried, ‘This holy leaf will take us across the river.’ And with this, he jumped on it and immediately began to drown. Then, another friend caught him by the neck. However, the friend recalled certain words of wisdom: ‘When total destruction is imminent, a wise man sacrifices half and works with the rest.’ So he concluded, ‘He should be cut into two!’ And they cut the friend they had saved into two halves with a sharp sword and moved on. [2] It is easy to see that these learned fools had all the right knowledge, but they did not know how to use it correctly to solve real-life problems. So, Richard Feynman is right. A highly educated person can be stupid because education makes an intelligent person smarter, but a stupid person a bigger idiot.

Question: If you do something that you know it's wrong, but then confess and try to make amends, but the other person rejects your apology and blows you off, what should you do then?
Answer: The Chinese philosopher Lao Tzu once said, “Watch your thoughts, they become your words; watch your words, they become your actions; watch your actions, they become your habits; watch your habits, they become your character; watch your character, it becomes your destiny.” We can represent this wisdom in the form of the following diagram. In short, our thoughts decide our destiny. It is important to understand that no one does good or bad things accidentally. We do good things when we are good inside and bad things when we are inherently bad. If you are caught doing the wrong thing, like cheating on your spouse or telling lies, you lose your credibility with all the people who trust you. And it is difficult to gain trust once you lose it. A person who knows what is right and yet fails to perform the right action is weak in character and untrustworthy. Hence, our life experience suggests that if you forgive him, he will never learn his lessons and repeat the same actions again, with more caution and secrecy so that he is not caught again. He also knows now that even if he is caught again in the wrong act, he will be forgiven. Hence, people find it difficult to forgive when they catch their loved ones cheating on them and doing wrong things. Apology is not a matter of right but at the discretion of the person who is wronged by you. You can be forgiven only when the person believes that you have realised your mistakes and changed yourself to become a trustworthy person. Hence, the best way to seek forgiveness from people is not by words but by action. If you really change yourself and become a good person discarding all the bad habits, people will see the difference and they may forgive you for your past mistakes. Your mistakes may be forgiven, but will never be forgotten. Please read this Aesop’s Fable. A Countryman’s son by accident trod upon a Serpent’s tail, which turned and bit him so that he died. The father in a rage got his axe, and pursuing the Serpent, cut off part of its tail. So the Serpent in revenge began stinging several of the Farmer’s cattle and caused him severe loss. The Farmer thought it best to make it up with the Serpent, and brought food and honey to the mouth of its lair, and said to it: “Let’s forget and forgive; perhaps you were right to punish my son, and take vengeance on my cattle, but surely I was right in trying to revenge him; now that we are both satisfied why should not we be friends again?” “No, no,” said the Serpent; “take away your gifts; you can never forget the death of your son, nor I the loss of my tail.” Moral of the story: Injuries may be forgiven, but not forgotten.[1] The poet Rahimdas has beautifully said, Rahiman dhaga prem ka, mat todo chatkaya, Tute se phir na jude, jude ganth pad jaya. English translation Don't snap the delicate thread of love between people. If it breaks once, it cannot be mended. Even if you mend it there will be a knot in it. Hence, the best thing is to never do wrong things deliberately and break the hearts of your loved ones, because if your action hurts someone you love, you can never regain the same love again.

Question: What are the potential drawbacks of being wealthy? Is it worth it to have a lot of money?
Answer: Almost everyone in the world seeks wealth as it is commonly believed that the more wealth we have, the more happiness we shall enjoy in life. However, the wealthiest people are often not the happiest since wealth, like any other commodity, follows the law of diminishing marginal returns. The law can be graphically displayed in the following graph.[1] Wealth provides you great happiness in the initial phase, as you can use wealth to fulfil your needs of food, water and clothing and lead a comfortable life by purchasing a big house, luxury cars, expensive gadgets etc. While there is no limit to earning wealth, there is a limit to our ability to enjoy the goods purchased with wealth. Hence, you soon come to the second phase, and the excess wealth fails to provide you proportional happiness. For instance, if you have lots of money, you can enjoy eating anything you like, without any restriction on quantity. When you have the tastiest food before you, it is almost impossible to control your temptation to eat more than what you require. The result is that soon, you become obese and get inflicted with numerous diseases. Question: Is it true that most poor and middle class humans participate in religious activities more than rich humans?
Answer: In 2009, an international organisation, Gallup, surveyed 114 countries. The global median proportion of adults who say religion is an important part of their daily lives is 84%. However, the study also found an interesting correlation between religion and per-capita income. While only 5% of the poorest (per capita income 0-$2000) considered religion unimportant in their lives, 52% of the people above the income of $25,000 considered religion unimportant. Question: Why do people downplay the difficulty of the UPSC exam to those who have taken it or are preparing for it?
Answer: UPSC examination is just an examination. Most people can’t clear the UPSC examination even after exhausting all their attempts because they don’t have the right aptitude and the right preparation strategy. Let me give you my own example. After completing my B Tech, I joined Larson and Toubro in 1987. However, after realising that I didn’t like corporate jobs, I decided to take the UPSC civil services examination. Due to family conditions, I could not afford to stay home and prepare, so I chose to do an M-Tech from IIT Delhi in 1988 and simultaneously prepare for UPSC. In those days, a large number of civil servant aspirants used to join IIT Delhi for the civil services examination. There was, of course, no guidance from IIT regarding UPSC, and hardly anyone used to join any coaching for UPSC. I joined IIT Delhi in July 1988 in “Design of Mechanical Equipment” and simultaneously started UPSC preparation. I did not choose Mechanical Engineering as my graduation subject; instead, I chose mathematics and physics as optional subjects. I started UPSC preparation from scratch in 1988 and was able to not only complete my M Tech with 8.54/10 Grade points but also get selected on the first attempt in IRS with a 272 rank in the 1989 UPSC examination. Hence, I did not find UPSC difficult at all. However, I was not the only person who cracked UPSC on his first attempt while doing M Tech with all new optional subjects. Many aspirants did even better and even got a rank within the top 20 with the same level of preparation. If you ask them, they would perhaps say that UPSC is a cakewalk. At the same time, I know many aspirants who kept writing UPSC for several years, exhausted all their attempts and failed to clear their Mains. For them, nothing is more difficult than cracking UPSC. Some people consider UPSC a matter of luck, a lottery, to console themselves that they missed UPSC due to their bad luck. However, I know many people who wrote UPSC 4 times and got selected with a better rank every time. Hence, when someone says that UPSC is easy, they are not lying. UPSC is indeed relatively easy for many people. If you have the right aptitude and you prepare with the proper strategy, you can indeed crack UPSC easily in your first attempt itself.[1] However, if you don’t have the most appropriate aptitude but keep working hard for UPSC, you may crack it after a couple of attempts, like Anudeep Durishetty, who got first rank on his 5th attempt.[2] Hence, instead of blindly following the herd, it would be advisable to assess your aptitude and ability for UPSC and get the right guidance for your UPSC preparation.

Question: Why doesn't everyone dream big?
Answer: You perhaps know this man. He is Byju Raveendran, the founder of India’s highest-valued startup Byju’s. He dreamt big and founded ByJu’s, which was once valued at around $23 Billion. The company has raised over 5 billion [1]from investors and is now set to face an insolvency resolution process at the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). According to the Forbes Billionaire Index 2024, Raveendran’s net worth also went down to zero.[2]He is responsible for loosing 5 billion of investors wealth and is now being accused of cheating millions of students for not provinding them the promised qualityof education. He also dreamed big and became the Chief Minister of Delhi within months of forming his political party. Today, he is languishing in jail for several months for corruption. Many people in the world dream big. It is easy to dream big. It is, however, difficult to realise big dreams. Our dreams are nothing but our desires. When our desires are big, we are not satisfied even if we have enough wealth or power to live a happy life. The difference between our desires and reality creates a gap, which results in dissatisfaction and frustration that makes our lives miserable. Many people are willing to make all types of compromises, including breaking the social, moral and legal norms to realise their dreams. However, even if they realise their dreams, their past mischiefs don’t let them live in peace and catch up them very soon. Soon, they lose everything that they built over their lifetime and live a frustrated life. Our dreams should be realistic, and we should be able to achieve them with some effort without compromising our values and principles. We can keep raising the standards of our dreams if we attain our earlier dreams by fair means with a clear conscience. The most important thing is to live a happy and peaceful life, which does not require dreaming big and achieving great things. Big dreams are a euphemism for greed in the modern language, which are often the source of suffering and frustration rather than of happiness and peace. The German-American social psychologist and philosopher Erich Fromm wisely said, “Greed is a bottomless pit that exhausts the person in an endless effort to satisfy the need without ever reaching satisfaction.” It is good that everyone does not dream big, since that will only make the competition stiffer and realisation of dreams more difficult for everyone. It is also good for everyone that many people choose to remain happy with whatever they have rather than dream big, become greedy, and make their lives miserable in their attempt to fulfil their big dreams. Question: What is your opinion on the saying 'If you love someone, set them free'?

While you may not be concerned so much about hundreds of people dying in a remote part of the world, you are concerned if your loved one is hurt even a bit. In the same way, if your loved ones achieve success in life or are happy, you feel successful and happy for them. If you love someone, not only does their joy and sorrow become your own, but you also feel responsible for their joy and sorrow. Hence, it is your duty to act in the best interest of your loved ones, and this may sometimes mean disciplining them if they are going down the wrong path or doing something that will harm them. Let us take some examples. There is a valuable lesson in the following Aesops’ Fable. A boy stole a lesson book from one of his schoolfellows and took it home to his Mother. She abstained from beating him. The next time, he stole a cloak and brought it to her, and she again commended him. The youth advanced to adulthood and stole things of still greater value. At last, he was caught in the very act and, having his hands bound behind him, was led away to the place of public execution. His Mother followed in the crowd and violently beat her breast in sorrow, whereupon the young man said, "I wish to say something to my Mother in her ear." She came close to him, and he quickly seized her ear with his teeth and bit it off. The Mother upbraided him as an unnatural child, whereon he replied, "Ah! if you had beaten me when I first stole and brought to you that lesson book, I should not have come to this, nor have been thus led to a disgraceful death."[1] There can be serious consequences for freeing your loved ones. Question: Can you describe the experience of being an IAS or IRS officer in India? Is there a sense of happiness and satisfaction in this role?
Answer: I have been an IRS officer for 25 years (1991–2016). My experience as an IRS officer has been quite good. The reasons are as follows. As an IRS officer of Indirect Taxes (Customs, GST & Narcotics), you get exposure as a tax officer, adjudicator, police officer (Narcotics and Anti-smuggling) and as educator and trainer (in Academies). Here is my old picture in uniform as a Deputy Commissioner of Customs and Central Excise. In civil services, IAS is still the best service, as you get exposure to almost every department of the state and central government. As an IAS officer, you have to face political interference, frequent transfers, long working hours and poor work-life balance. Hence, if you join either IAS or IRS, you are likely to be happy and satisfied, provided you learn to value what you have rather than lamenting on the negative aspect of your service by focusing your mind on what you lack.

Question: Why do we Indians give so much importance to government jobs?
Answer: There are many things that are determined more by tradition than by reality. Indians prefer government jobs because their parents and parent’s parent and their parents prefered government jobs. However, if you apply your mind, you'll see that the reality is quite different now. In the past, indeed government jobs were the best, much better than any private sector jobs. Let me give my own example. After my B Tech in Mechanical Engineering in 1987, from IIT (BHU) Varanasi, I got a job in L&T, which was considered to be among the most prestigious companies in India. This company used to be the dream company of almost half the students of IIT Bombay, Mechanical Engineering. I joined the company in Bangalore and worked there for one year. Do you know the salary of the Graduate Engineer Trainee (GET) then? It was only Rs 1550 + Rs 300 (HRA) per month. Back then, the starting salary of a civil servant was Rs 2500 plus government accommodation plus a phone (which used to be a very expensive and luxury item then) and a government car. To achieve the matching level of facilities and perks, you have to work for at least 15 years in L&T. In in 1980s, the Indian economy was driven by the public sector and government officials were in the driver's seat. However, the situation has changed in the last three decades. While not every student of an IIT gets a great salary, in the year 2022, 960 IIT graduates received Rs 50 lakh and above annual pay.[1] This amount is much more than the starting salary of an IAS officer, which is less than Rs 10 lakhs per annum. Even a top civil servant at the rank of cabinet secretary would not get this much of a salary. Pension was another great advantage of government services in the past. For example, a top civil servant who retired in 1990 would be getting a salary of around Rs 10,000 pm and so his pension would be around Rs 5000. However, the same civil servant, if alive today, would get a pension of more than Rs 200,000 pm today. Even after his death, his wife/spouse would get half of this amount as a pension. No private sector can match this even today. However, this Old Pension Scheme has been withdrawn since 2004 and is no longer available to government officers including IAS today. No wonder, many youngsters, who have been brought up in metro cities and educated in top colleges are not interested in government jobs today, as they have much better options available today. It is thus evident that government jobs have lost much of their sheen and are no longer the top choice for the most brilliant Indians. However, government jobs are still preferred by millions of Indians who do not have the right exposure and still take their decisions based on their parent’s wishes and value the social value of the job more than the real nature of the job. Government jobs are still important because they still provide greater job security than the private sector and you can’t be removed easily after you are appointed. Moreover, due to the high corruption in some government jobs, the officers can make so much illegal money that no employee in the private sector can even dream of. However, such jobs and such corrupt government officers are few in number and when they are caught, they end up paying huge prices for their corruption. Unfortunately, it is also not easy to work honestly in most government jobs that people aspire to, as honest officers face lots of problems including transfers, if they follow the rules and are honest. Unfortunately, the level of politicians has declined tremendously over the last few decades and it is becoming increasingly difficult to work independently in accordance with the law. In my view, if you are truly brilliant, government jobs are no longer the best option for you. Instead, you must try to get a private sector job in a top Indian or Multinational company in India or in a developed country. If you join a government job without knowing the present reality, based on the glory of the past, you may be highly disappointed and become frustrated in your future. Government jobs are good today only if you prefer job security and are not hesitant to become part of the system.

Question: Why should I help others? If I don't, what will be the consequences?
Answer: When I was young, we used to spend our summer vacations in our native village in Raibereli. In those days, almost all marriages used to take place in the summer because it is cheaper to arrange a marriage in the summer than in the winter when you have to arrange for warm clothes, quilts etc. Marriage in the village in those days used to be celebrated like a festival. Instead of hotels, the Barat (marriage party) used to stay in gardens under lush green trees. In place of procuring bedding and utensils from the tent house, we used to borrow them from our relatives and other villagers. There would be no hired cooks or waiters in the marriage. All the members of the clan would be participating in the preparation of the food. While men would be cutting and chopping the vegetables, women folks would prepare the chapatis (bread) and purées (fried bread). Instead of waiters, the family members and the villagers would be serving the food themselves to the guests. The cost of arranging marriage was thus quite low as all services were free. However, marriages happen in different ways in cities, and things have changed even in the villages. My daughters got married a few years ago. We booked the hotel, caterers, cars etc. Since we were staying in a different city, we flew to the city for a marriage function just two days before. Neither we nor the guests had any work to do since all preparations were done by the hotel staff and caterers. They had to only dress up and get ready to participate in various functions of the marriage and do the necessary rituals. Almost all guests departed the next day of marriage and we also left the place within two days of marriage. The effort required for the arrangement of the marriage of my daughter was much lesser compared to what used to take place in the village, and it was much superior. However, arranging marriage in a hotel costs many times more money than the marriages organized in the village. The arrangement of marriage in a village appears quite romantic, beautiful, and economical. However, now even in the villages, the marriage functions are not arranged in the old way as the economic conditions of people have improved. There are no free lunches in the world and certainly, there are hidden costs and obligations when we receive help from someone for free. When you accept the help of the family and society members, you bound yourself with the obligation to provide free services whenever marriage takes place in their families. If you fail to fulfil your obligation, you will suffer criticism, condemnation and exclusion from the society. On the other side, when you make all the arrangements using professionals, you pay the market rates for the services and there is no further obligation from either side. There is no need to help other people if you don’t need their help. Helping random people shall not help you in the time of your need. Help those, like family, friends, close relatives, and neighbours, who may help you back at the time of your need. When you help others selflessly, you also expect selfless help from other, which does not usually come in real life. When your life depends on the help of others, you feel helpless, angry and frustrated when help does not come. It is good to be kind and helpful to people in their time of need, but it is not an obligation on you unless you have taken help from them or hope to take their help in future. You must first help yourself by earning and saving enough money so that when the time comes, rather than seeking any help from anyone, you can pay for all the services that you need from people, and live a good life. You must always help those who have helped you in past. You may help the strangers only when you feel they need it and they are also ready to help themselves. It is often said that even God help those who help themselves. Source of pictures: Google Images

Question: Is it possible a good human may do bad things or an ex criminal may do good things later in their lives?
Answer: It is not only possible but most probable. As a matter of fact, in statistics, there is a well-laid-down principle called “regression toward the mean” (also called reversion to the mean, and reversion to mediocrity). According to this principle, the phenomenon where if one sample of a random variable is extreme, the next sampling of the same random variable is likely to be closer to its mean.[1] Hence, a good human being is more likely to commit bad things in future and a bad person is more likely to commit good things in future. Let us look at the spring in the picture, pressed by both hands You have reduced the length of the spring by applying external force. How long can you press this spring? As soon as you release the pressure, the spring will go to the other extreme, and then gradually come back to its natural state, and surely have a longer length (original) as compressed to its length in the pressed state. Similarly, if you elongate the spring with external force, again it will return to its natural state, as soon as it is released and become shorter. Human nature is composed of both good and evil. What we call evil is actually the original nature of the person (basic instinct), while what we call good is cultivated in human beings through education and training (learned instinct). Throughout our lives, we have to balance our good and evil nature to lead a natural life. When you suppress the original nature of the person by force, it is like pressing the spring, which always tries to come back to the original self as soon as the opportunity arises. Similarly, if you have been doing bad things in life, like engaging in crime or corruption, you feel very uncomfortable in your subconscious mind due to the guilt and you try to do something good to overcome your guilt and acquire your original conscience (also called prayaschit in Sanskrit meaning getting back to prior/original conscience). It has been my experience that in the real world, honest people are more inclined to become corrupt because they see them enjoying their lives with huge ill-gotten wealth (which they always lack). On the other side, the corrupt and wealthy people envy the honest people who are trusted, admired and loved by others and sleep well due to their clear conscience and honest living. Unfortunately, crime and corruption are a one-way path. An honest person can become corrupt or criminal by a single action, but a criminal and corrupt person can never become a good person even if does numerous good deeds. It is always easy to fall, but difficult to rise. Hence, if you have been a good person, don’t allow the temptation and lust to commit evil acts. And if you have done bad things in life, it is never too late to become a good person. Saint Augustine said so wisely, “Every saint has a past and every sinner has a future.” Source of picture: Google Images

Question: What are some interesting & amazing facts that most people don't know?
Answer: Let me share with you something amazing that I learned recently. Please answer the following question. Approximately 1% of women aged 40-50 have breast cancer. A woman with breast cancer has a 90% chance of a positive test from a mammogram, while a woman without has a 10% chance of a false positive result. What is the probability a woman has breast cancer given that she just had a positive test? When I was asked this question, I thought this to be a simple problem. I did my mental calculation and my estimate was around 70–80%. Perhaps, your estimate is also something close. Even experts also gave similar estimates. When ninety-five physicians were asked this question their average answer was 75%. [1] However, we are not only wrong in our estimation of the probability but so grossly wrong that it may surprise us. The correct answer is that the woman has just a 8% chance of having breast cancer. So, what is happening? How come even the experts are so wrong about the calculation of the real chances of getting breast cancer? The misjudgement happens because of our tendency to ignore relevant statistical information in favour of case-specific information. Instead of taking into account the base rate or prior probability of an event, we are often distracted by less relevant information. Our inability to consider the prior probability or the base is also called the base rate fallacy. In statistics, base rate refers to the percentage of a population that has a specific characteristic. If we take a random individual and there’s no additional information, the base rate tells us the likelihood of them demonstrating that characteristic. In this case, we have not taken into account the fact that only 1% of women have breast cancer. Let me explain how to understand and solve this problem. Suppose that the sample size is 1000. Since only 1% of the women have breast cancer, hence, there would be 10 women with breast cancer and 990 women without breast cancer. When these 990 women were tested, 99 got positive cancer reports without any cancer, while 9 women who actually got cancer reported correctly. Hence, while only 10 women have cancer, the total number of detection would be 99+9=108. Hence, the probability of those who have been tested positive and have breast is just 9/108 which is around 8%. I found this piece of knowledge truly amazing. The correct calculation of the probability is done by Bayesian inference in which Bayes' theorem is used to update the probability for a hypothesis as more evidence or information becomes available. Bayesian inference uses prior knowledge, in the form of a prior distribution in order to estimate posterior probabilities. You can solve this problem directly by using Bayes’ formula. The knowledge of the base rate fallacy is essential for correctly estimating the possibility and avoiding wrong decisions in life. For example, one lesson is that you must not undertake routine tests for a disease like breast cancer which is quite less prevalent, unless you have symptoms. Moreover, if you test positive in such cases, better to get tested again to avoid a false positive. Some examples of operating base rate fallacy are as follows. I hope you have found this information interesting and useful, and you can use this to find answers to many problems in your life and take the correct decisions.

Question: How common are regrets among people? Is it possible to live a life without any regrets?
Answer: Regret is a bad habit, and unfortunately, it is widespread. The Australian caregiver Bronnie Ware based on her experiences in palliative care gave the following regrets in her book, The Top Five Regrets of the Dying: A Life Transformed by the Dearly Departing Regrets happen when we either take decisions in a hurry, or fail to value what we have achieved and focus only on what we missed. I, however, find regret a total waste of time and an emotion that comes usually due to ignorance of the facts. Most regrets arise due to hindsight bias, which is a psychological phenomenon in which one becomes convinced they accurately predicted an event before it occurred. It happens when a person looks back at an event and believes they predicted the outcome, even if they failed to act on that "prediction." Unfortunately, this leads people to think that their judgment is better than it is. Most people fail to understand the idea that once we know the outcome, it’s much easier to construct a plausible explanation.[2] Most people are great at finding scapegoats to blame for their failures. When people find no external scapegoat, they make their past-selves their scapegoats to protect their present-selves, to feel better. In reality, you are only fooling yourself through regrets, as you remain as intelligent or foolish as you were earlier. Suppose you regret because you bought a stock whose value has come down or remained stagnant, and thus you make a loss, as compared to your possible investment in some other portfolio. How could you have known at the time of investment how the stock is likely to behave in future? However, once the outcome is known, it is easy to blame your past-self for your past decisions. Question: Does repeating a lie over and over make it the truth?

Take, for instance, the following Joke, which went viral some years ago. I told my son, “You will marry the girl I choose.” He said, “NO!” I told him, “She is Bill Gates’ daughter.” He said, “OK.” I called Bill Gates and said, “I want your daughter to marry my son.” Bill Gates said, “NO.” I told Bill Gates, My son is the CEO of the World Bank.” Bill Gates said, “OK.” I called the President of the World Bank and asked him to make my son the CEO. He said, “NO.” I told him, “My son is Bill Gates’ son-in-law.” He said, “OK.”[1] As you can see from the above story, a series of interconnected lies actually became the truth because they were all spoken with intelligence, keeping the psychology of the listeners in mind. For instance, these leaders were the most popular leaders in their country at their time, thanks to the lies spread by them to fool the masses. Likewise, when people falsely start projecting a person as a fool, corrupt, inefficient, or ignorant and criticising a good person, gradually, the people start believing so, and the person indeed starts behaving strangely and foolishly. Many good people, like Jesus Christ and Socrates, were perceived as evil at their time, thanks to the repeated lies told about them. A horse is certainly considered to be more gifted than an ass, but it does not mean that he is more lucky, as evident from the following Aesop’s Fable. A Horse and an Ass were travelling together, the Horse prancing along in its fine trappings, the Ass carrying with difficulty the heavy weight in its panniers. “I wish I were you,” sighed the Ass; “nothing to do and well fed, and all that fine harness upon you.” The next day, however, there was a great battle, and the Horse was wounded to death in the final charge of the day. His friend, the Ass, happened to pass by shortly afterwards and found him on the point of death. “I was wrong,” said the Ass.[1] Hence, our lives depend on what we think, say, and do, rather than what we are born with or what we acquire through luck or chance. The gains by luck are similar to the gains by tossing the coin, which eventually even out. Ultimately, our life depends on our own hard work, sincerity, commitment and grit. The former American president Thomas Jefferson said aptly, “I’m a great believer in luck, and I find the harder I work, the more I have of it.” We are the makers of our own lives and creators of our own luck and destiny.

Question: Why is life so hard for good people?
Answer: Let us compare the lives of two types of people. The first category of people are those who are enjoying their lives daily. They enjoy the best food, eat as much as they can, do not workout at all, binge drink alcohol and do everything that give them pleasure. The second type of people are those who are facing hard lives every day. They walk, run or workout daily, eat nutritious food in limited quantity, avoid intoxicants and everything that may look very tempting, but is bad for their physical, moral or intellectual health. Now fast forward their lives by a few decades. The first category of person is suffering from numerous diseases, and the doctors have prohibited him from eating almost everything that he loves to eat. He spends most of his time running around doctors and does not live long. The second category of person is fit as a fiddle. He still suffers the pain of working out every day, but he can still eat everything he loves, looks good for his age and lives long. This is exactly what happens to good and bad people. You have the choice to select the good or bad actions. You have, however, no choice to select the consequence of your action, that will follow according to the law of nature and you shall reap what you sow. Source of pictures: Google Images

Question: If given a choice, what would you like to have? Money or power?
Answer: I prepared for the civil services examination at IIT Delhi, which used to be UPSC's garh (centre) those days (around 1990). The toppers of GATE from Northern India used to get admission to IIT Delhi in whichever branch they could get into, and then they used to prepare for CSE while doing their M-Tech. One of the most prospective IAS was my hostel neighbour Satyendra Gupta (SG), who was the all-India topper of GATE on Mechanical Engineering and a Gold Medalist in IIT Roorkee. He, like us, joined IIT Delhi to prepare for IAS. However, after a couple of weeks, when I visited his hostel room, I saw no UPSC books on his table. On being asked, he told me that he dropped the idea of writing UPSC, “I will do M Tech and attempt getting 10 point grades. Then I will do PhD from the US and become a professor.” When I tried to persuade him to write UPSC, he asked, “Why do you want to go for UPSC?” I parroted the standard reply, “Because, as a civil servant, you enjoy great power and the best perks like vehicles and big government houses.” He replied back, ‘I disagree. Power is a great responsibility and you can’t enjoy it unless you misuse it. As an IPS officer, you have to work round the clock, fight criminals and hardly get proper sleep at night. As an IAS officer, you deal with filthy politicians, corrupt contractors and officers within the department. If you take action, you make enemies and if you don’t use power, you lose all respect. Similarly, there is no fun in having a government vehicle, which is only for the official purpose, unless you misuse them for personal use.’ I did not agree with his views then and chose to become a civil servant, while Satyendra chose his path and is now a professor at the University of Southern California. However, after working for more than 25 years as an IRS officer, I now agree with him. Power is not a privilege, but a great responsibility. Whenever you exercise your power against anyone, you make them your personal enemies and you are hated for it. However, if you fail to exercise your power you are still hated for being incompetent and useless. For instance, most people hate Modi because he exercises his power to the fullest. People also hated Dr Manmohan Singh because he did not exercise his powers. Most people seek power because they can (mis)use power to make money, intimidate their rivals or become popular. When such people are caught, or voted out by people, they lose their power, money and prestige in society. On the other side, money can provide you lasting happiness and peace of mind, if earned through legal and moral means. While you can lose power anytime (You may be a PM/CM/DM today and a nobody tomorrow), money is more secure, if invested properly. Power is, therefore, desired mostly by poor and middle-class people, who want to feel important in the eyes of society and secretly believe that they can make lots of illegal money through corruption. However, if you are rich, you rarely seek power, as money itself is a power besides being a means to enjoy your life. You might have seen the children of many top politicians and civil servants starting a company or joining top companies to make lots of money. However, you would rarely find the children of top businessmen writing civil services examinations or joining politics to acquire power. When I understood the folly of power, I left the IRS when I had 11+ years of job left. Hence, If I am given a choice, I will choose money (lawfully earned) over power any day.
